title: Cells: the building blocks of life
goal: Students can say what a cell is, put the levels from cell to organism in order, and name what four cell parts do.

scenes.say: Welcome to Pet Town. In this lesson you will find out what cells are, how they team up to build a whole living thing, and what a few important cell parts do.

show.text: Cells: the building blocks of life
show.sub: Biology Unit 1 · Cellular organization and cell parts

say: Here is the big idea. Every living thing is made of cells. A cell is the smallest unit that is alive.
Some living things are just one cell. A bacterium is a whole living thing made of a single cell. It eats, grows, and makes more bacteria, all inside that one cell.
Other living things are made of many cells. A mushroom, an oak tree, and your dog are each made of millions or even trillions of cells.
And new cells always come from cells that already exist. A cell splits to make new cells.

show.heading: Every living thing is made of cells
items: A cell is the smallest unit that is alive
One cell: a bacterium does every life job by itself
Many cells: a mushroom, a tree, a dog
New cells come from cells that already exist

say: In a many-celled living thing, cells are organized in levels. It starts with a single cell, like one muscle cell.
A group of similar cells working together is a tissue. Many muscle cells together make muscle tissue.
Different tissues working together make an organ. Your heart has muscle tissue, nerve tissue, and other tissues.
Organs working together make an organ system. The heart and blood vessels together move blood around your body.
All of the organ systems working together make the organism: the whole living thing.

show.heading: From cell to organism
items: Cell: the smallest living unit
Tissue: similar cells working together
Organ: different tissues working together
Organ system: organs working together
Organism: the whole living thing

say: Let's follow one example. Your stomach is lined with cells.
Those cells form stomach tissue, and different tissues form the stomach, which is an organ.
The stomach, the intestines, and the liver work together as the digestive system.
And the digestive system works with your other systems to keep you, the organism, alive. If one system stops working, the others have trouble too.

show.heading: Example: your stomach
items: Stomach cells
Stomach tissue → the stomach (an organ)
Stomach + intestines + liver = the digestive system
All the systems together = you, the organism

say: Now let's look inside a cell. Every cell has a cell membrane. It is the outer layer that controls what goes in and what comes out.
Inside is the cytoplasm, a jelly-like fluid where most of the cell's work happens.
Most cells have a nucleus. It holds the cell's DNA, the instructions for everything the cell does.
Mitochondria release energy from food, so the cell has the energy it needs to do its jobs.
Plant cells also have a cell wall, which gives them a stiff shape, and chloroplasts, which use sunlight to make food.

show.heading: Cell parts and their jobs
items: Cell membrane: controls what goes in and out
Cytoplasm: the jelly where the cell's work happens
Nucleus: holds DNA, the cell's instructions
Mitochondria: release energy from food
Plant cells only: cell wall (support) and chloroplasts (make food from sunlight)

scenes.say: Your turn. Pause the video and choose your answer.
scenes.answer: The answer is cell, tissue, organ, organ system. Similar cells make a tissue, tissues make an organ, and organs make an organ system.

say: Let's sum up. Every living thing is made of one or more cells.
Cells build tissues, tissues build organs, organs build organ systems, and systems build the organism.
Each cell part has a job, from the membrane on the outside to the nucleus in the middle. Now go practice in Pet Town!

show.heading: What to remember
items: All living things are made of cells
Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism
Each cell part has its own job
